content: In mathematics and logic, an operation refers to a specific action or procedure that generates a new value from one or more input values. Operations are categorized into two primary types: unary and binary. Unary operations involve a single input value. Examples of unary operations include negation (e.g., changing the sign of a number) and trigonometric functions such as sine or cosine. Binary operations, in contrast, require two input values. Common examples of binary operations include addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and exponentiation. Operations are not limited to numbers; they can also involve other mathematical objects. For instance, logical values like true and false can be combined using logical operations such as and, or, and not. Vectors can undergo operations like addition and subtraction. Rotations in geometry can be combined through function composition, where one rotation is performed followed by another. In set theory, operations include binary operations like union and intersection, as well as unary operations like complementation. For functions, operations such as composition (combining two functions) and convolution (used in signal processing) are common. It is important to note that operations are not always defined for every possible input value. For example, in the set of real numbers, division by zero is undefined, and the square root of a negative number is not a real number. The set of input values for which an operation is defined is called its domain. The set of all possible output values is referred to as the codomain, while the actual set of values produced by the operation is called the range. For example, the squaring operation in real numbers produces only nonnegative values. In this case, the codomain is the set of all real numbers, but the range is restricted to nonnegative real numbers. Operations can also involve objects of different types. For example, a vector can be multiplied by a scalar (a single number), resulting in another vector. Similarly, the inner product of two vectors produces a scalar value. Operations may exhibit specific properties, such as associativity (e.g., addition and multiplication of numbers), commutativity (e.g., a + b = b + a), anticommutativity (e.g., the cross product of vectors), or idempotence (e.g., applying the same operation multiple times yields the same result). The inputs to an operation are referred to as operands, arguments, or inputs, while the resulting value is called the result, output, or value. Operations can involve any number of inputs, ranging from zero to many. For example, a nullary operation (an operation with zero inputs) simply produces a fixed value from the codomain. Unary operations have one input, binary operations have two inputs, and in general, an operation with k inputs is called a k-ary operation. Formally, an operation is defined as a function of the form ω: X₁ × X₂ × ... × Xₖ → Y, where X₁, X₂, ..., Xₖ are the domains of the operation, Y is the codomain, and k (a non-negative integer) is the arity or type of the operation. A unary operation has an arity of one, a binary operation has an arity of two, and so on. A k-ary operation is a specific type of (k+1)-ary relation that is functional on its first k domains. This definition typically applies to finitary operations, which involve a finite number of inputs (k). However, the concept can be extended to include operations with infinite arity, where the inputs are indexed by an infinite set. In many cases, the term operation implies that the domain of the function is a Cartesian power of the codomain (e.g., S × S → S for binary operations on a set S), but this is not a universal requirement. The distinction between operation and operator often depends on the context. For example, one might refer to the operation of addition when focusing on the inputs and outputs, but use the term addition operator when emphasizing the process or the abstract function itself.
